claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous electrophysiology research.

claims.claim: The gene expression data suggest that the rectifying Kv channel also exists in a chondrostean fish, supporting the hypothesis that non-teleost electroreceptor physiology is conserved.
claims.source: Our gene expression data suggest that this channel also exists in a chondrostean fish, supporting the hypothesis that non-teleost electroreceptor physiology is conserved (at least across jawed vertebrates), and identify Kv1.5 and Kvβ3 as the candidate channel.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the gene expression data and previous electrophysiology studies.

claims.claim: Kv1.5 and Kvβ3 are identified as the candidate rectifying Kv channel in non-teleost ampullary organs.
claims.source: Our gene expression data suggest that this channel also exists in a chondrostean fish, supporting the hypothesis that non-teleost electroreceptor physiology is conserved (at least across jawed vertebrates), and identify Kv1.5 and Kvβ3 as the candidate channel.
claims.evidence: This is based on the gene expression data showing ampullary organ-specific expression.

claims.claim: The sequence of paddlefish Kcna5 predicts several amino acid substitutions in highly conserved regions of Kv1.5 that could affect its properties.
claims.source: The sequence of paddlefish Kcna5 predicts several amino acid substitutions in highly conserved regions of Kv1.5 that could affect its properties.
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of the cloned gene.

claims.claim: The S4 segment of voltage-gated ion channels is the voltage sensor and is highly conserved.
claims.source: The S4 segment of voltage-gated ion channels is the voltage sensor, and is highly conserved (Barros et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: In paddlefish Kv1.5, the first positively-charged amino acid in the voltage sensor (R1 position) has been replaced by a threonine (T357).
claims.source: The first positively-charged amino acid in the voltage sensor is normally arginine: since it is the first arginine in S4, it is referred to as the R1 position. In paddlefish Kv1.5, this has been replaced by a threonine (T357).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 6J.

claims.claim: Experimental substitution of methionine at the R1 site in Drosophila Shaker decreases the gating charge on the channel and the slope of the conductance voltage curve.
claims.source: Experimental substitution of methionine at this site in Drosophila Shaker (R362M; Aggarwal and MacKinnon, 1996) decreases the gating charge on the channel and the slope of the conductance voltage curve (Aggarwal and MacKinnon, 1996; Elliott et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: R1 forms a seal with hydrophobic residues in S2 that keeps ions from flowing around the S4 segment.
claims.source: Aside from its role as part of the voltage sensor, R1 forms a seal with hydrophobic residues in S2 that keeps ions from flowing around the S4 segment: substitution of R1 in Drosophila Shaker with histidine (R362H) allows protons to leak past S4 (Starace and Bezanilla, 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Substitution of R1 in Drosophila Shaker with some amino acids allows monovalent cations to leak past S4 when the cell is hyperpolarized (omega current).
claims.source: Substitution with some other amino acids (alanine, cysteine, serine, valine) allows monovalent cations to leak past S4 when the cell is hyperpolarized (omega current) (Tombola et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: It is not known if a threonine at the R1 position would encourage an omega current, but an omega current could act like a slow depolarizing leak current, possibly contributing to the spontaneous activity of ampullary electroreceptors.
claims.source: It is not known if a threonine at this position would encourage an omega current, but an omega current could act like a slow depolarizing leak current, possibly contributing to the spontaneous activity of ampullary electroreceptors.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on known properties of omega currents.

claims.claim: A variety of studies indicate that the end of the S3/S4 linker and the top of S4 contact the top of S2, S3 and S5/pore in the closed or open state.
claims.source: A variety of studies indicate that the end of the S3/S4 linker and the top of S4 contact the top of S2, S3 and S5/pore in the closed or open state (Kanevsky and Aldrich, 1999; Elliott et al., 2004; Soler-Llavina et al., 2006; Henrion et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2011; Elliott et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Generally speaking, amino acid substitutions at some of these positions cause a rightward shift in the conductance-voltage curve, meaning that the channel would open at more depolarized voltages.
claims.source: Generally speaking, amino acid substitutions at some of these amino acid positions cause a rightward shift in the conductance-voltage curve, meaning that the channel would open at more depolarized voltages.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge from previous research.

claims.claim: Characterization of the effects on Kv1.5 of the various amino acid substitutions in paddlefish will require future channel expression in a heterologous system and mutagenesis studies.
claims.source: Characterization of the effects on Kv1.5 of these various amino acid substitutions will require future paddlefish channel expression in a heterologous system and mutagenesis studies: for example, characterizing the properties of paddlefish Kv1.5, as compared with paddlefish Kv1.5 in which these amino acids (in different combinations) have been substituted with conserved residues, and/or substituting the paddlefish-specific amino acids into, for example, human Kv1.5.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about future experimental approaches needed.

claims.claim: Genes that are required for synaptic transmission at the hair cell (but not photoreceptor) ribbon synapse are also expressed in larval paddlefish ampullary organs.
claims.source: Furthermore, genes that are required for synaptic transmission at the hair cell (but not photoreceptor) ribbon synapse are also expressed in larval paddlefish ampullary organs.
claims.evidence: This is based on the gene expression data presented in the study.

claims.claim: The data suggest very close developmental and, most likely, evolutionary links between hair cells and electroreceptors.
claims.source: This suggests very close developmental and, most likely, evolutionary links between hair cells and electroreceptors.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the shared gene expression patterns.

claims.claim: The selective pressure for the evolution of electroreceptors is likely related to the transition from filter-feeding to predation in the lineage leading to vertebrates.
claims.source: The selective pressure for the evolution of electroreceptors, which enable the detection of living animals in water, is likely related to the transition from filter-feeding to predation in the lineage leading to vertebrates (Gans and Northcutt, 1983; Northcutt and Gans, 1983; Northcutt, 2005b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Various lines of evidence support the homology of all non-teleost electroreceptors, including those of lampreys.
claims.source: Various lines of evidence support the homology of all non-teleost electroreceptors, including those of lampreys: their stimulation by weak, low-frequency cathodal fields (and inhibition by strong cathodal fields); their innervation by pre-otic anterior lateral afferents projecting to the dorsal octavolateral nucleus in the hindbrain; and, in jawed vertebrates, their demonstrated embryonic origin, together with neuromasts, from lateral line placodes (Bullock et al., 1983; Northcutt, 1992; Braun, 1996; New, 1997; Baker et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The striking similarities in both development and physiology identified in paddlefish ampullary organs are consistent with electroreceptor evolution in the vertebrate ancestor either via the diversification of hair cells that had already evolved from ancestral mechanoreceptor cells, or via the diversification of an ancestral mechanoreceptor cell into both hair cells and electroreceptors.
claims.source: Given this, the striking similarities in both development and physiology that we have identified in paddlefish ampullary organs are consistent with electroreceptor evolution in the vertebrate ancestor either via the diversification of hair cells that had already evolved from ancestral mechanoreceptor cells (Duncan and Fritzsch, 2012; Fritzsch and Straka, 2014), or via the diversification of an ancestral mechanoreceptor cell - with an apical primary cilium (lost in lamprey electroreceptors), microvilli, and synaptic ribbons (Northcutt, 1986; Bodznick, 1989; New, 1997), and using otoferlin, Vglut3 and Cav1.3 channels for synaptic transmission - into both hair cells and electroreceptors.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the data and supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The unbiased RNA-seq approach has shed new light on molecular mechanisms underlying ampullary organ development and physiology in a non-teleost chondrostean fish.
claims.source: Our unbiased RNA-seq approach has shed new light on molecular mechanisms underlying ampullary organ development and physiology in a non-teleost chondrostean fish.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement about the overall contribution of the study.

claims.claim: The expression in ampullary organs of key hair cell transcription factor genes and genes encoding proteins specifically required for glutamate release at the hair cell ribbon synapse supports close developmental and physiological, hence evolutionary, relationships between electroreceptors and hair cells.
claims.source: The expression in ampullary organs, as well as neuromasts, of key hair cell transcription factor genes, such as Atoh1, Sox2 and Pou4f3, and genes encoding proteins specifically required for glutamate release at the hair cell ribbon synapse, such as otoferlin, Vglut3 and Cav1.3 channels, supports close developmental and physiological, hence evolutionary, relationships between electroreceptors and hair cells.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gene expression data.

claims.claim: The identification of the first-reported ampullary organ-specific genes provides novel insight into the potential molecular basis of ampullary organ-specific development and physiology.
claims.source: Our identification of the first-reported ampullary organ-specific genes, including the proneural transcription factor gene Neurod4, a beta-parvalbumin gene, and voltage-gated potassium channel subunit genes, provides novel insight into the potential molecular basis of ampullary organ-specific development and physiology.
claims.evidence: This is based on the identification of differentially expressed genes in the study.

claims.claim: Cav1.3 (with Cavβ2) is identified as a candidate for the apical voltage-sensing channel in paddlefish ampullary organs.
claims.source: We identify Cav1.3 (with Cavβ2) as a candidate for the apical voltage-sensing channel (indeed, Cav1.3 was recently shown to be the voltage-sensing channel in skate electroreceptors; Bellono et al., 2017), and Kv1.5 (with unusual amino acid substitutions that may affect its properties), together with Kvβ3, as a candidate for the basal membrane rectifying Kv channel predicted from skate ampullary organ electrophysiology.
claims.evidence: This is based on the gene expression data and supported by a recent study in skate.

claims.claim: Kv1.5 (with unusual amino acid substitutions that may affect its properties), together with Kvβ3, is identified as a candidate for the basal membrane rectifying Kv channel predicted from skate ampullary organ electrophysiology.
claims.source: We identify Cav1.3 (with Cavβ2) as a candidate for the apical voltage-sensing channel (indeed, Cav1.3 was recently shown to be the voltage-sensing channel in skate electroreceptors; Bellono et al., 2017), and Kv1.5 (with unusual amino acid substitutions that may affect its properties), together with Kvβ3, as a candidate for the basal membrane rectifying Kv channel predicted from skate ampullary organ electrophysiology.
claims.evidence: This is based on the gene expression data and previous electrophysiology studies.

claims.claim: The analysis has provided wide-ranging insights into molecular aspects of ampullary organ development and physiology, and an essential framework for future comparative work.
claims.source: Overall, our analysis has provided wide-ranging insights into molecular aspects of ampullary organ development and physiology, and an essential framework for future comparative work to determine both the function of these genes, and the extent to which they are conserved across other non-teleost electroreceptive vertebrate groups.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement about the overall contribution of the study.

results.result: RNA-seq differential expression analysis of paddlefish stage 46 opercula (containing ampullary organs and neuromasts) versus fins (no lateral line organs) identified 490 lateral line-enriched genes, of which 334 were assigned to specific genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C40 describe the experimental design and results of the RNA-seq analysis. The approach is clearly described with appropriate tissue selection (opercula vs fins), developmental stage (stage 46), and differential expression threshold (1.85-fold). The annotation results showing 334 assigned genes out of 490 total are presented as data. This represents a standard transcriptomic approach with clear methodology.

results.result: Key hair cell transcription factors including Atoh1, Sox2, Pou4f3, and SoxB1 family members (Sox1, Sox3) are expressed in developing paddlefish ampullary organs as well as neuromasts, suggesting conservation of the transcriptional network regulating both lateral line organ types.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C44-C73 are supported by in situ hybridization data (Figures 2A-P) showing expression of these transcription factors in both ampullary organs and neuromasts at multiple developmental stages. The validation confirms genes from the RNA-seq dataset and includes previously reported genes. The inference about network conservation (C74) is reasonable given the shared expression patterns, though functional validation would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Neurod4, a proneural bHLH transcription factor, is the first gene identified to be expressed specifically in ampullary organs but not neuromasts, suggesting it may be involved in specifying ampullary organ/electroreceptor fate.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C75, C85-C89 are strongly supported by in situ hybridization data (Figure 3A-F) showing Neurod4 expression exclusively in ampullary organs from stage 39 onward, with no expression in neuromast lines. This represents the first reported differential expression between these organ types (C90). The speculation about fate specification (C91, C113) is reasonable given Neurod4's known proneural functions in other systems (C77-C82), though functional validation is needed.

results.result: Potential Neurod4-interacting transcription factors Pou4f1, Lhx3, and Myt1 are expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts, suggesting additional factors beyond Pou4f1 control differential Neurod4 expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C95, C102, C109 are supported by in situ hybridization data (Figure 3G-I) showing expression of these genes in both organ types. The inference that additional factors control Neurod4 differential expression (C96) is logical since Pou4f1 (which can repress Neurod4 in other systems, C92) is expressed in both organ types while Neurod4 is ampullary organ-specific. However, the speculation about Lhx3-Neurod4 interaction (C103) requires experimental validation.

results.result: The vesicular glutamate transporter Vglut3 (encoded by Slc17a8) is highly enriched (30.9-fold) and expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts, indicating electroreceptors use glutamate as their neurotransmitter.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C121 are supported by RNA-seq data and in situ hybridization (Figure 4A). The inference that electroreceptors use glutamate (C122-C123) is well-supported by: (1) Slc17a8 expression data, (2) Vglut3's essential role in hair cell glutamate loading (C118), and (3) previous electrophysiology showing 'glutamate-like' neurotransmitter release in skate (C26). This provides molecular confirmation of prior physiological observations.

results.result: Otoferlin (encoded by Otof, 20.9-fold enriched) is expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts, suggesting electroreceptor synaptic vesicle exocytosis is otoferlin-dependent like hair cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C129 are supported by RNA-seq data and in situ hybridization (Figure 4B). The inference about otoferlin-dependent exocytosis in electroreceptors (C130) is reasonable given: (1) otoferlin's unique requirement for hair cell exocytosis (C124-C125), (2) its expression in paddlefish ampullary organs, and (3) the presence of ribbon synapses in electroreceptors. However, functional validation would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Cacna1d (encoding Cav1.3, 19.3-fold enriched) is expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts, identifying Cav1.3 as a candidate for both the apical voltage-sensing channel and basal neurotransmitter release channel in electroreceptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C137 are supported by RNA-seq data and in situ hybridization (Figure 4C). The inference about Cav1.3 mediating glutamate release basally (C138) is well-supported by its known role in hair cells (C131, C133-C134). The hypothesis about apical voltage-sensing (C148, C212) is supported by: (1) paddlefish expression data, (2) electrophysiology in skate showing L-type Ca channels in apical membrane (C145), (3) recent identification of Cav1.3 in skate electroreceptors (C146), and (4) requirement for apical Ca conductance in sturgeon (C147).

results.result: Cacnb2 (encoding Cavβ2, 2.7-fold enriched) is expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts with seemingly stronger expression in ampullary organs, suggesting Cavβ2 may be the auxiliary beta-subunit for Cav1.3 channels in electroreceptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C143 are supported by RNA-seq data and in situ hybridization (Figure 4D). The inference about Cavβ2 as the auxiliary subunit (C144) is reasonable given: (1) its known role regulating Cav1.3 in hair cells (C140), (2) expression in paddlefish ampullary organs, and (3) apparently stronger expression in ampullary organs than neuromasts. However, the visual assessment of 'stronger expression' is qualitative and would benefit from quantification.

results.result: Rims2 (15.7-fold enriched) and Ctbp2/Ribeye are expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts, suggesting these synaptic ribbon-associated proteins function similarly in electroreceptors and hair cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C153, C159 are supported by RNA-seq data and in situ hybridization (Figure 4E-F). The Ribeye-specific probe design (recognizing only the A-domain) is appropriate. The inferences about Rims2 involvement in Cav1.3 recruitment (C154) and Ribeye as a key ribbon component (C160) are reasonable given their known functions in hair cells (C151, C155-C157). However, Ctbp2 not being in the enriched dataset (C158) while still being expressed suggests it may be more broadly expressed.

results.result: The mechanisms of neurotransmission at the electroreceptor ribbon synapse are essentially identical to those at the hair cell ribbon synapse, involving otoferlin-dependent exocytosis of Vglut3-loaded synaptic vesicles in response to Cav1.3 channel activation.
results.evaluation: This synthesis claim (C161) is well-supported by the combined expression data for Slc17a8/Vglut3, Otof/otoferlin, Cacna1d/Cav1.3, Rims2, and Ctbp2/Ribeye in ampullary organs. The prediction of conservation across non-teleost ampullary organs (C162) is reasonable given their established homology. This represents a major advance in understanding electroreceptor physiology, though functional validation of these molecular components would strengthen the conclusions.

results.result: Pvalbβ1/Ocm (22.8-fold enriched) is expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts, and phylogenetic analysis places it in the beta-parvalbumin clade containing mammalian oncomodulins.
results.evaluation: Claims C163, C175-C176 are supported by RNA-seq data, phylogenetic analysis (Figure 5A), and in situ hybridization (Figure 5B). The phylogenetic analysis appropriately uses Bayesian methods with a relaxed molecular clock to root the tree without an outgroup. The classification as a beta-parvalbumin related to oncomodulins is well-supported. The citation to skate data (C177) showing high Pvalb8 expression provides comparative context.

results.result: Pvalbβ2 (2.1-fold enriched) is expressed specifically in ampullary organs but not neuromasts, representing a second ampullary organ-specific gene that may be involved in ampullary organ-specific Ca2+ regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C178-C180 are supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 5A) and in situ hybridization (Figure 5C) showing ampullary organ-specific expression at all stages examined. This represents the second identified ampullary organ-specific gene after Neurod4. The speculation about Ca2+ regulation (C181) is reasonable given parvalbumins are Ca2+-buffering proteins (C164) and different hair cell subtypes have different parvalbumin complements (C166), though functional validation is needed.

results.result: Kcna5 (encoding Kv1.5, 12.4-fold enriched) and Kcnab3 (encoding Kvβ3, 21.4-fold enriched) are expressed specifically in ampullary organs, identifying them as candidates for the basal membrane rectifying Kv channel predicted from skate electrophysiology.
results.evaluation: Claims C182-C184 are supported by RNA-seq data and in situ hybridization (Figure 6A-H) showing ampullary organ-specific expression beginning at stages 38-39. The identification as candidates for the rectifying Kv channel (C192, C213) is well-supported by: (1) ampullary organ-specific expression, (2) electrophysiology evidence for such a channel in skate (C190), (3) known properties of Kv1.5 and Kvβ3 in other systems (C185-C186), and (4) voltage oscillations recorded in paddlefish (C189). The speculation about optimal properties for membrane oscillation (C187-C188) is reasonable but requires functional validation.

results.result: Paddlefish Kv1.5 has several amino acid substitutions in highly conserved regions including replacement of the R1 position in the voltage sensor with threonine (T357), which may affect channel properties.
results.evaluation: Claim C193 is supported by sequence analysis (Figure 6J) showing multiple substitutions. The R1 substitution (C195) is clearly documented. The discussion of potential functional consequences (C196-C199) appropriately cites relevant mutagenesis studies in Drosophila Shaker. However, the statement that characterization 'will require' future studies (C202) acknowledges that functional effects remain speculative. The sequence analysis is thorough, but the functional implications require experimental validation.

results.result: The close developmental, physiological, and evolutionary links between electroreceptors and hair cells are supported by shared expression of key transcription factors and synaptic transmission genes, consistent with electroreceptor evolution via diversification of hair cells or a common mechanoreceptor ancestor.
results.evaluation: This synthesis claim is well-supported by the extensive gene expression data showing shared developmental regulators (Atoh1, Sox2, Pou4f3, etc.) and synaptic transmission machinery (Vglut3, otoferlin, Cav1.3, Ribeye) between ampullary organs and neuromasts. The evolutionary inference (C208) appropriately presents two alternative hypotheses and is supported by citations to previous work on electroreceptor homology (C207). However, this remains an inference from molecular similarity rather than direct evolutionary evidence.

results.result: Gene Ontology analysis of the lateral line-enriched dataset shows binding activities represent ~39% of function hits, catalytic activities ~35%, and transmembrane-associated activities ~19%.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43 are supported by the GO analysis presented in Figure 1. The percentages are clearly stated and the categorization is standard. This provides a functional overview of the enriched gene set, though it is primarily descriptive rather than hypothesis-testing.

results.result: Background claims about lateral line system composition, evolutionary history, morphology, and current state of knowledge are presented to establish context for the study.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C23 are primarily background knowledge supported by appropriate citations to previous literature. These establish the scientific context including: lateral line system composition (C1), model organism limitations (C2), evolutionary patterns (C13-C16), morphological distinctions (C19-C21), and knowledge gaps (C23). These are well-established facts in the field and appropriately cited.

results.result: Prior work on electroreceptor physiology and molecular biology is reviewed, establishing that understanding of ribbon synapse function and ion channel identity in electroreceptors was limited before this study.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C35 review prior work on electroreceptor synapses and physiology, appropriately citing previous studies. The statement about limited molecular understanding (C32-C33) is supported by the literature review. The limitation of candidate gene approaches (C35) provides justification for the unbiased RNA-seq approach. These claims establish the rationale for the current study.

results.result: The selective pressure for electroreceptor evolution is likely related to the transition from filter-feeding to predation, and various lines of evidence support homology of all non-teleost electroreceptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C206-C207 are supported by appropriate citations to previous evolutionary and comparative studies. These provide evolutionary context for interpreting the molecular similarities observed in the study. The homology argument is important for justifying predictions about conservation across non-teleost species.

results.result: The unbiased RNA-seq approach has provided wide-ranging insights into ampullary organ development and physiology, identifying the first ampullary organ-specific genes and establishing a framework for future comparative work.
results.evaluation: These summary claims (C209, C211, C214) are supported by the collective results of the study. The identification of ampullary organ-specific genes (Neurod4, Pvalbβ2, Kcna5, Kcnab3) and shared developmental/physiological genes represents significant advances. The statement about providing a framework for future work is appropriate given the comprehensive dataset generated.
